tldr: This paper presents InstantMimic, a system that redesigns the reinforcement learning loop to be GPU-native, eliminating critical bottlenecks to train complex humanoid motor skills in just seconds. Taking advantage of this ultra-fast training speed, it also makes fully autonomous hyperparameter search using an LLM agent practical.
hero_caption: Training progression for walk, spinkick, and backflip skills. In an astonishingly short real-world wall-clock time of just 1.5 to 2.6 seconds, the humanoid goes from falling over to mastering complex, highly dynamic motor skills.
overview:
Physics-based character control, which trains characters to produce realistic motions inside a physics simulator, has become a core technology not only in computer graphics but also in modern humanoid robotics. In particular, imitation learning methods that track reference motions (such as DeepMimic) are powerful, but training these policies has traditionally demanded lengthy computation times. While GPU-parallel simulation became widespread with platforms like Isaac Gym, practical real-world training efficiency has remained bottlenecked.

When the authors thoroughly profiled an existing training pipeline (based on Isaac Lab), they uncovered a surprising fact: the execution bottleneck was not the physics solver itself. Instead, it stemmed from fragmented GPU kernel invocations and CPU memory access that triggered CPU-GPU synchronization stalls right on the critical path. Even though physics ran quickly on the GPU, the hardware sat idle for most of the remaining time.

To solve this, the authors developed InstantMimic, a fully GPU-native system that unifies simulation, observation generation, reward computation, policy inference, and PPO policy updates within a single execution flow. Built on MuJoCo Warp as its backend, it rigorously leverages kernel fusion (merging multiple operations into a single GPU function), CUDA Graphs, and the complete elimination of CPU-GPU synchronization.

Experiments showed that not only walking and running, but also acrobatic full-body behaviors like backflips and cartwheels can be learned in just 1.5 to 4.5 seconds. Furthermore, because a full training run finishes in seconds, they demonstrated a practical workflow where an LLM agent autonomously iterates and discovers optimal hyperparameters through trial and error.
contributions: Identified through system-level profiling that the true bottleneck in physics-based deep RL loops is not the physics solver, but GPU kernel fragmentation and CPU memory synchronization stalls on the critical path.

Dramatically reduced the training time for diverse dynamic skills from minutes or hours down to a few seconds by keeping the entire loop—from simulation to reward computation and PPO updates—resident and fused on the GPU.

Turned autonomous LLM-agent-driven hyperparameter optimization into a practical framework, where the agent plans, proposes, and evaluates experiments in closed-loop cycles made feasible by second-scale training runs.
Open-sourced the fully GPU-native framework code to ensure reproducibility and accelerate future robotics and animation research.

sections.heading: Why is reinforcement learning still slow despite GPU simulators?
sections.summary: Physics-based character control is foundational to modern humanoid development, but slow training has long been a challenge. The root cause of slow training—despite GPU simulators—lies in pipeline inefficiencies outside the physics solver.
sections.details:
Physics-based character control drives characters and robots inside physics simulations. Because policies must satisfy complex dynamical constraints, it is far more challenging than kinematic approaches; however, it excels at adapting to contact-rich environments and producing realistic motions. In recent years, imitation learning based on Deep Reinforcement Learning (Deep RL), popularized by DeepMimic, has become the dominant approach, expanding beyond computer graphics to agile motor skill acquisition for full-sized humanoid robots.

However, the greatest barrier to such systems remains computational training cost. Recent GPU-parallel physics simulators were expected to accelerate learning dramatically, yet running end-to-end training loops still severely underutilizes GPU hardware. When the authors profiled a representative imitation learning pipeline in detail, they discovered that the primary bottlenecks did not come from the physics solver calculations, but from the surrounding pipeline.

Specifically, two factors dominate: GPU kernel fragmentation caused by frequent, unbatched, fine-grained GPU operations, and CPU memory access stalls on the critical path introduced by Python-level abstractions. In this work, the authors fundamentally redesign the entire training loop from a systems perspective, proposing InstantMimic—a system that integrates simulation, state construction, reward evaluation, and policy updates in a unified, GPU-native flow. As a result, learning motor skills that once required tens of minutes to hours now completes in just a few seconds.

captions.F1: Real-world wall-clock training time for each dynamic skill. Walk converges in 1.5 seconds, spinkick in 1.9 seconds, and backflip in 2.6 seconds, transitioning rapidly from falling over to following stable motion trajectories.

sections.heading: Core principles of GPU-parallel simulation and GPU optimization
sections.summary: Accelerating robot learning has advanced through GPU-parallel physics engines, but unlocking full hardware performance requires overcoming overheads inherent to parallel computing. Faster training also transforms how we approach hyperparameter search.
sections.details:
### 2.1. GPU-accelerated Physics Simulation
Research in physics-based control historically evolved using rigid-body simulators such as ODE and the CPU version of MuJoCo. However, on-policy reinforcement learning algorithms like PPO require massive amounts of environmental interaction, making simulation throughput the primary constraint. Addressing this challenge, Isaac Gym and Brax ran dynamics calculations massively in parallel on GPUs, drastically reducing humanoid controller training from days to minutes. This work builds its system on MuJoCo Warp, a next-generation GPU-native foundation.

### 2.2. Optimization Principles in GPU Computing
To fully harness the massive parallel compute of a GPU, three major parallel computing overheads must be addressed:
- **Kernel launch overhead**: Launching a function (kernel) on the GPU from the CPU introduces a fixed latency of several microseconds. When many tiny operations are launched sequentially, CPU invocation latency outstrips GPU compute time, leaving the GPU idle. Kernel fusion (merging multiple operations into one) and CUDA Graphs (recording a sequence of launches to replay in one shot) resolve this issue.
- **Data movement**: On modern hardware, moving data is far more expensive than computation itself. Eliminating unnecessary tensor copies via in-place operations is essential, both across the CPU-GPU boundary and within GPU memory.
- **Synchronization**: Attempting to read GPU data from the CPU forces the CPU to wait until all preceding GPU work finishes, which completely stalls the GPU pipeline.

While prior systems like Madrona pursued GPU-native simulation primarily for game environments, InstantMimic differs by fully unifying everything from 3D multi-DoF humanoid physics to the PPO training loop.

### 2.3. Hyperparameter Optimization for Deep RL
Reinforcement learning is notoriously sensitive to hyperparameters. Traditional Bayesian optimization and Population Based Training (PBT) require many evaluations, forcing practitioners to manually narrow search spaces under black-box constraints. While recent efforts employ Large Language Models (LLMs) as search agents to intelligently modify code and configurations, InstantMimic's ability to train in seconds makes this LLM-driven autonomous search practical for the first time.

sections.heading: Profiling the baseline: GPUs sat idle 77% of the time
sections.summary: Profiling a standard RL loop in Isaac Lab revealed that the GPU is idle or stalled for 77% of each step's execution time. Kernel fragmentation outside the physics solver and CPU-GPU synchronization are the primary culprits.
sections.details:
### 3.1. Low GPU Utilization from GPU Kernel Fragmentation
In an RL rollout step, it is widely assumed that the physics engine consumes most of the execution time. However, profiling the Isaac Lab baseline revealed the exact opposite. Remarkably, the physics calculation (physics phase) accounted for only 32% of a single rollout step, while subsequent operations—reward computation, environment resets, observation creation, and buffer writes (post-physics phase)—consumed 64%.

Looking closer, action application within the physics phase ate up 29% on its own, leaving pure physics simulation responsible for just 22.3% of the total step. During the non-physics processing, effective GPU utilization plummeted to an average of only 7.3%. This severe drop is caused by GPU kernel fragmentation: sequentially dispatching dozens of small PyTorch tensor operations from Python causes CPU kernel launch overhead to dominate execution time, creating gaps where the GPU constantly waits for its next instruction.

### 3.2. CPU Memory Access in Critical Path Stalls the GPU
Another critical inefficiency is GPU stalling triggered by data exchange between the CPU and GPU. When a CPU-GPU transfer occurs on the critical path of the rollout loop, the GPU is forced to halt all execution until the transfer completes.

Profiling uncovered two inconspicuous yet fatal patterns in the code:
- **State reads from CPU buffers**: When constructing observation tensors, internal Isaac Lab APIs (such as `body_com_pose_b`) referenced simulation buffers on the CPU side and copied them to the GPU on every step. This alone caused the GPU to stall for roughly 15.9% of the total step time.
- **Calling .item() for control flow**: When evaluating episode termination conditions, the done flags were computed on the GPU, yet `.item()` was called to extract a scalar to the CPU to evaluate a Python `if` condition. That single `.item()` line triggered an explicit synchronization point, freezing the entire GPU pipeline.

sections.heading: GPU-native architecture: kernel fusion and zero CPU synchronization
sections.summary: To eradicate these bottlenecks, the system adopts MuJoCo Warp, fuses GPU kernels, applies CUDA Graphs, and completely eliminates CPU synchronization across the entire training pipeline.
sections.details:
### 4.1. Reducing GPU Kernel Fragmentation
To address kernel fragmentation, the authors evaluated four implementation strategies on the reward computation phase:
1. **vanilla**: Sequential standard PyTorch tensor operations (the baseline).
2. **jit**: Partially fused kernels via PyTorch JIT (as used in Isaac Lab). Execution time dropped from 281 μs to 112 μs (a 2.5× speedup), but kernel launch gaps remained.
3. **cgraph**: CUDA Graphs applied to eliminate launch overhead gaps between kernels, achieving an execution time of 29 μs (a 9.7× speedup).
4. **warp**: Full JIT compilation of the entire reward function into a single GPU kernel using NVIDIA Warp.

In this Warp version, intermediate tensor allocations were eliminated and only a single kernel launch was required, slashing execution time to 3.14 μs. This represents an astonishing 89.7× (nearly two orders of magnitude) speedup over vanilla PyTorch. Consequently, InstantMimic implements the entire post-physics phase as explicit Warp kernels and uses PyTorch's `torch.compile` to fuse kernels within the PPO policy update phase.

### 4.2. Removing CPU Memory Access from the Critical Path
CPU memory accesses were completely banished from the rollout loop, recovering the ~16% GPU stall time observed in the baseline.

Specifically, leveraging MuJoCo Warp's design where internal state arrays reside in GPU memory from the start, observation generation kernels were rewritten to read GPU arrays directly. In addition, episode resets no longer branch via Python `if` statements. Instead, reset calculations execute unconditionally for all environments, updating values only for terminated environments via a GPU binary mask. This 'unconditional execution + masking' pattern completely eliminates all synchronization points that previously transferred data back to the CPU mid-loop.

sections.heading: Training in seconds enables autonomous LLM agent optimization
sections.summary: With training finishing in seconds, manual tuning becomes the new bottleneck. To address this, the authors introduce a fully autonomous hyperparameter optimization loop where an LLM agent plans strategies, proposes parameters, and executes experiments.
sections.details:
When an RL experiment finishes in mere seconds, the research and development bottleneck shifts from algorithmic computation to human idle time: waiting for a person to inspect results, adjust parameters, and relaunch runs. Manual trial-and-error cannot keep pace with such immense compute speeds. To bridge this gap, this work constructs a closed-loop hyperparameter optimization (HPO) framework where an LLM agent iterates autonomously.

This optimization loop consists of three stages:
1. **plan**: The LLM reviews past trial history, the current best configuration, and overall strategic goals, updating its search strategy in natural language regarding which hyperparameter groups to focus on next.
2. **propose**: Guided by the updated strategy, the LLM outputs concrete candidate hyperparameter values formatted as JSON.
3. **experiment**: A Python script receives the proposed values, benchmarks InstantMimic across multiple random seeds, logs results, and updates the best-known parameters.

The human only provides the success criteria and stopping conditions. Unlike random or grid search, the LLM applies domain knowledge to make nuanced decisions—such as reasoning that training accelerated but pose error worsened, calling for reward weight adjustments, or recognizing that a parameter hit the upper bound of its search range and expanding the search boundary accordingly.

sections.heading: Experimental results: 5 complex skills learned in seconds with up to 5.8× throughput
sections.summary: InstantMimic delivers roughly 4× to 6× higher frame throughput than baselines, mastering skills from walking to acrobatic stunts in seconds. It also pre-trains on large motion datasets in just 30 minutes.
sections.details:
### 6.1. Implementation Details
Experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. The MuJoCo Warp simulator was used to train reference motion tracking for a humanoid character. The reward function uses a DeepMimic-style multiplicative formulation combining errors in joint angles, velocities, center of mass, and end-effector positions/orientations, optimized via PPO.

### 6.2. Training Performance for Motion Tracking
Comparing training throughput on the backflip task, Isaac Lab (PhysX) achieved 0.105 Mfps (~105k frames/sec) and mjlab (MuJoCo Warp) reached 0.157 Mfps, whereas InstantMimic achieved 0.613 Mfps. This corresponds to an impressive 5.85× speedup over Isaac Lab and 3.91× over mjlab.

Furthermore, running 80 cycles of hyperparameter search with an LLM agent (GPT-5.5-high) on the backflip task reduced active training time to reach success from an initial 18.77 seconds down to 2.17 seconds (an 8.6× improvement). Using these optimized settings across five diverse reference motions (walk, run, spinkick, backflip, cartwheel), all skills converged to target accuracy within 1.5 to 4.5 seconds. Even the challenging cartwheel, which requires inverted balance and complex hand-foot contact transitions, was mastered in only 4.5 seconds.

### 6.3. Analysis of the LLM Search
Analyzing the LLM agent's search revealed sophisticated decisions beyond the reach of standard Bayesian optimization. For example, it reasoned about why a specific metric degraded and switched its focus to different hyperparameters, or autonomously widened search intervals when optimal values clustered near boundaries—mirroring the flexible reasoning of human expert researchers at machine speeds.

### 6.4. Scaling to Large Motion Datasets
The system also scales beyond single motions to large datasets. Pre-training a VAE-based latent controller on 37.4 hours of motion capture data (AMASS) matched the success rate of prior work (PHC) in just 30 minutes. Moreover, training downstream navigation policies on this latent space to reach target waypoints achieved high control performance (reaching 8.2 goals per 10 seconds) with only 1 minute of additional training.

captions.F8: Qualitative tracking results for five dynamic motions learned with InstantMimic (from top to bottom: walk, run, spinkick, backflip, cartwheel). The humanoid reproduces acrobatic aerial flips and complex alternating ground contacts smoothly without falling.

sections.heading: Conclusion: the real bottleneck in RL was outside the simulation
sections.summary: This study demonstrates that full-pipeline GPU optimization enables second-scale skill training and autonomous LLM-driven optimization. When training becomes this fast, controller design paradigms fundamentally change.
sections.details:
This work reconsiders the design of deep reinforcement learning for physics-based control from a systems architecture perspective. Profiling revealed a critical truth: the true bottleneck was not the physics solver, but kernel fragmentation and CPU synchronization in the surrounding infrastructure. By leveraging direct GPU-resident memory access and optimized kernel fusion, rollout overheads were almost entirely eliminated.

As a result, complex full-body acrobatics can now be trained in seconds, and pre-training on massive motion datasets takes only 30 minutes. Among the five evaluated motions, the cartwheel was the most difficult due to alternating hand-foot contacts and body inversion, requiring ~4.5 seconds—still exceptionally fast compared to ~1.5 seconds for walking and running.

In addition, this ultra-fast loop makes autonomous hyperparameter search with LLM agents genuinely practical. Slashing backflip training time from 18.77 seconds to 2.17 seconds across 80 autonomous cycles highlights a new workflow for robot controller development. When the computational cost of an experiment drops this low, development will shift from human trial-and-error to autonomous machine-driven exploration and optimization.

sections.heading: Appendix: LLM agent prompt design and search reproducibility
sections.summary: The LLM agent operates autonomously under cleanly structured prompts, and experiments confirm that open-weight models achieve comparable optimization capability.
sections.details:
### A.1. Agent Interface and Search Protocol
The LLM agent execution loop is managed by a Python runtime infrastructure. The LLM is given no direct file access or tool execution privileges; it interacts strictly through prompt inputs and outputs. The prompt includes task definitions (objectives and ranking criteria), tunable parameter lists, current best settings, and the trial history of the last 15 cycles alongside cross-seed variance. When the LLM outputs a strategy in Markdown and proposed parameters in JSON, the Python runner validates parameter bounds before executing multi-seed training and benchmarking.

### A.2. Backflip Search & Model Comparison
For the backflip task, the objective was to minimize the median time required across three seeds to reach target tracking success (90% success rate). Over an 80-cycle search, the best configuration (2.17 seconds training time) was discovered at cycle 65.

To evaluate search robustness, five independent 80-cycle searches were conducted using GPT-5.5-high, yielding a highly consistent median best training time of 2.291 seconds (interquartile range IQR: 0.095 seconds). Furthermore, when tested with the open-weight model GLM-5.2-high under the same protocol, it achieved a strong median of 2.530 seconds (IQR: 0.571 seconds), with one run logging the overall fastest time of 1.748 seconds. This confirms that the autonomous search framework operates effectively without being locked into proprietary commercial models.

takeaways: Even when using GPU-parallel simulators, non-physics components in an RL pipeline (observation building, reward evaluation, `.item()` synchronization, etc.) can waste the vast majority of GPU time (77% in this paper's baseline).

Rather than dispatching uncoordinated PyTorch operations, applying kernel fusion (e.g., via NVIDIA Warp), CUDA Graphs, and completely removing CPU synchronization yields dramatic multi-fold to order-of-magnitude throughput improvements.
When mastering complex humanoid skills takes only seconds, fully automated trial-and-error by LLM agents becomes practical, fundamentally transforming the robot controller design workflow.
limitations: Because the HPO objective focused solely on minimizing the time to reach target success rates, faster convergence occasionally came at the expense of joint tracking accuracy (pose precision), highlighting challenges in multi-objective optimization design.
The system relies heavily on MuJoCo Warp; porting existing complex environments, robot assets, and sensor models written for Isaac Lab or PhysX requires non-trivial reimplementation effort.
While the training loop takes only seconds, overhead outside the loop—such as environment initialization, checkpoint serialization, and evaluation—becomes relatively more prominent.
